tip: Inside an 'att' clause, adverbs like 'aldrig' normally come before the verb: 'att hon aldrig skulle glömma'.
The adjective adds '-a' when the subject is plural: 'vi är glada' (we are happy).
When a clause comes first, the main verb goes before its subject: 'hinner vi' (we make it).
'Som om' plus a past verb means as if: 'som om tiden stod stilla' (as if time stood still).
'Kommer att' plus an infinitive expresses the future: 'kommer att gå bra' (will go well).
'Vad' plus an adjective forms an exclamation: 'vad roligt' (how nice).
The '-s' ending can give a verb an each-other meaning: 'ses' means see each other, as in 'vi ses'.
Adding '-s' can form the passive: 'bjuds' means is offered, as in 'bjuds jag på fika'.
'Hit' means to here and marks motion, unlike the static 'här': 'kom hit' (come here).
'För att' plus an infinitive means in order to: 'för att hämta' (to pick up).
'Så att' introduces purpose, meaning so that: 'så att vi kan börja' (so that we can start).
'Sluta' plus a plain infinitive means stop doing something: 'sluta prata' (stop talking).
Swedish normally uses the definite form for body parts, not a possessive: 'tvätta händerna' (wash your hands).
'Lägga sig' means lie down or go to bed; the pronoun matches the subject: 'lägg dig' (go to bed).
Nationality adjectives stay lowercase in Swedish: 'svenska' (Swedish), not capitalized as in English.
'I och med att' is literally in and with that, but simply means given that or since.
'Huruvida' means whether and is formal. Everyday Swedish uses 'om' instead.
After 'är' the adjective agrees with the noun: ett-word 'huset' takes '-t', so 'stort', not 'stor'.
Swedish says 'ha rätt', literally have right, for to be right: 'hon har absolut rätt'.
The perfect uses 'har' plus the form 'gått': 'året har gått fort' (the year has gone fast).
Definite phrases double up: 'det' and the '-et' ending on 'slottet' both mean the, as in 'det gamla slottet'.
For a male person the definite adjective can end in '-e': 'den duktige läraren'. The '-a' form works too.
Definite adjectives normally add '-a' even when the base ends in '-t': 'tyst' becomes 'tysta' in 'det tysta rummet'.
Words like 'första' (first) count as definite: they take 'det' or 'den' and the '-a' form, as in 'det första steget'.
For emphasis Swedish uses 'det var X som' (it was X who), keeping the subject form: 'det var hon', not 'henne'.
For transport Swedish uses 'ta': 'hon tar bussen' (she takes the bus), 'tar tåget' (takes the train).
When 'som' is the object of its clause you can drop it: 'filmen vi såg' (the movie we saw).
The preposition stays at the end of the clause: 'rummet som vi sitter i' (the room we sit in).
The '-s' ending can give a verb an each-other meaning: 'vi träffas' means we meet each other.
'Komma ihåg att' means remember to and is followed by the infinitive: 'kom ihåg att låsa'.
